lead: Software is programs, data and documents; its type decides how it is engineered. Meter firmware, bank payroll and a UPI payment library are all software, each needing a different approach. This chapter defines software, contrasts it with hardware, lists application domains, defines legacy software and corrects six myths. This base makes process models sensible answers to particular products.
prereq: Nothing; this opens the unit. Process models follow in 1.4.

sections.h3: Software is programs, data and documents

blocks.text: Software is the collection of programs, data and documents that makes a computer useful. A program is instructions. Data is what the program reads or writes: a customer table, settings file, saved invoice. Documents describe the software: requirement note, design sketch, test cases, user manual. Delete the documents and the program still runs, but nobody can change it safely. Hence three parts, not one.

Software is developed, not manufactured. A factory makes identical hardware units; cost per unit falls with volume. Software is built once at the cost of people's time; each further copy costs almost nothing.

Hardware wears out from heat, dust and vibration; failure follows a bathtub curve: high at start, low middle, high end. Software does not wear out; it deteriorates. Every change risks breaking working behaviour, so failure climbs with modification unless code is cleaned. Cause is change, not use.

Software resembles other engineering in requirements, design, review, estimation, standards and client acceptance. It differs by being intangible, having no spare parts or manufacturing tolerance, being copied in seconds, and costing mostly human effort, not material.

sections.h3: Changing role, application domains and legacy software

blocks.text: Software's role has shifted from custom code for one client on one machine to four shapes. Product lines: one core sold to many by configuration. Software as a service: recurring fee for the vendor's running system, for example a GST filing portal; billed flat or per use. Embedded systems: software inside a device, such as electricity-meter firmware. AI-enabled systems: behaviour learned from data, used in fraud checks and recommendations. Each pushes engineering differently: reuse for product lines, timing and memory for embedded, data and model quality for AI.
Application domains group software by user and required behaviour:

items: System software: operating systems, compilers, drivers, file systems; serves other software.
Application software: payroll, inventory, booking, results portals. Web and mobile apps are treated separately here; some texts count them as a sub-class. Either is accepted, but be consistent.
Engineering and scientific software: CAD, circuit simulation, weather and structural models; heavy floating-point computation.
Embedded software: firmware reading sensors and driving actuators under real-time limits.
Product-line and reuse software: libraries, frameworks and components reused across products, such as a payment SDK.
Web and mobile applications: network-facing, many users and devices, short release cycles.
Artificial intelligence software: prediction and recommendation learned from data, not written by hand.

blocks.text: Legacy software is not a domain; it is a status: old software still in production and still business-critical. Ten or twenty years old, it runs on an outdated platform or language, few engineers understand it, documentation is incomplete, and changes are risky. Organisations keep it because it works, encodes business rules, and replacing it costs and risks more than maintaining it. A bank's core ledger is the usual example. A payroll system can be application software and also legacy. Options are to wrap it, re-engineer it, or replace it in phases (Unit 6).
A myth is a belief that sounds true and is false. Software myths excuse a shortcut already taken. They come from management, the customer and the practitioner.

head: Group and myth
Reality
rows: Management: adding programmers catches up a late project
Late additions add communication paths and training; the project slips further.
Management: an existing standards book covers quality
Standards must be tailored, taught and checked in reviews and audits.
Customer: general objectives suffice; details can come later
Missing requirements surface as rework, the costliest change.
Customer: requirements keep changing and change is easy
Change is easy to request and costly to absorb; evaluate and track each change.
Practitioner: once the program runs, the job is done
Maintenance starts at first delivery and lasts most of the product's life.
Practitioner: the only deliverable is working code
Design records, test cases and user documents are deliverables too.

blocks.text: Myths cost marks twice. Writing only the myth answers half; the correction carries marks. A team believing a myth skips reviews, documents or change control, then pays as rework.

examples.question: A Chennai IT firm maintains 40 applications: 25 custom web apps, 8 embedded firmware products, 5 reusable payment libraries, and 2 payroll systems that are 12 years old. (a) Classify all 40. (b) Identify legacy systems. (c) The 2 payroll systems have 5 engineers; the manager adds 3. Using communication paths n(n−1)/2, compute before and after and test the myth 'adding programmers catches up a late project'.
steps: 25 web apps serve end users over a network: application software, web and mobile sub-domain.
8 firmware products run inside meters and talk to hardware: embedded software.
5 payment libraries are built once and reused: product-line and reuse software.
2 payroll systems are application software; 12 years old, still in production and business-critical, so also legacy.
Extra paths = 28 − 10 = 18. Each path must be kept in sync; 3 newcomers need training.
The myth fails: the late project gains 18 communication paths and loses senior time to mentoring, so it usually finishes even later.
examples.answer: 27 application software (25 web apps plus 2 legacy payroll), 8 embedded and 5 product-line/reuse, 40 total; the 2 payroll systems are application software with legacy status; payroll paths grow from 10 to 28, an extra 18, so adding programmers does not catch up a late project.

traps: Writing 'software = program'. Software is programs plus data plus documents; documents make maintenance possible.
Calling any old program legacy. Legacy is old, in production and business-critical; unused two-year-old code is dead code.
Saying software wears out. Hardware wears out; software deteriorates because of change.
Listing a myth without the correction. Marks are for the corrected reality in one line.
Confusing 'developed, not manufactured' with 'free to produce'. Copying unit two is nearly free; building unit one is not.

quiz.q: Define software in one sentence and name its three parts.
quiz.a: Software is the collection of programs, data and documents that makes a computer useful; parts are programs (instructions), data (what is read or written) and documents (requirements, design, test cases, manuals).

quiz.q: Name four application domains of software.
quiz.a: Any four: system software, application software, engineering and scientific software, embedded software, product-line and reuse software, web and mobile applications, artificial intelligence software.

quiz.q: Software does not wear out, yet its failure rate rises over time. Explain why.
quiz.a: Hardware fails through physical wear such as heat and dust. Software fails through change: each modification can break working behaviour, defects accumulate, and documents drift from code. Failure rises with maintenance unless code is refactored.

quiz.q: Give one difference between system software and application software, with an example of each.
quiz.a: System software serves other software, for example an operating system or compiler; application software serves the end user's task, for example a payroll package or railway booking app.

quiz.q: A firm has 60 applications: 30 web apps, 12 embedded firmware, 10 reusable libraries and 8 systems over 15 years old that run the accounts. Classify them by domain and state the total.
quiz.a: Application software 38 (30 web/mobile plus 8 old accounts), embedded 12, product-line/reuse 10; 38 + 12 + 10 = 60. The 8 old accounts systems are not a separate domain; their status is legacy.

quiz.q: A late project has 6 engineers. The manager adds 4. Compute communication paths n(n−1)/2 before and after, and decide whether the myth holds.
quiz.a: Before: n = 6, paths = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15. After: n = 10, paths = 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45. Extra = 30 paths. The myth fails: 30 new channels plus training slow the team, so the project usually finishes later.

quiz.q: Why do organisations keep legacy software instead of replacing it at once?
quiz.a: It works and carries business rules built over years. Replacing it means re-deriving undocumented rules, retraining users and risking a critical service. Wrapping or phased re-engineering is cheaper.

quiz.q: State the myth 'we have a general objective, so we can start coding' and correct it in one line.
quiz.a: Customer myth: a general statement of objectives is enough to begin writing programs; details can be filled later. Reality: unclear requirements reappear as rework, the costliest change.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry treats software supply chains and open-source licences as a domain, because a product may be mostly third-party components. Machine learning makes data a first-class artefact, so 'software plus documents' often extends to 'software, data, documents and trained models'. Regulated sectors keep legacy systems alive for decades, so wrapping and re-engineering are steady jobs. Search next for software product lines, technical debt and Brooks's law.
